title: IMemoryCache for In-Memory Caching
description: Learn how to use IMemoryCache in ASP.NET Core to cache frequently accessed data in process memory with expiration policies and callbacks.

data.text: IMemoryCache is ASP.NET Core's built-in abstraction for storing data in the local process memory. When a controller or service requests data that is expensive to compute or retrieve, you can cache it in memory so subsequent requests return the result instantly — without hitting the database or external service.

MemoryCache is registered automatically when you call AddMemoryCache() on the IServiceCollection. The runtime stores entries in a concurrent dictionary backed by a least-recently-used (LRU) eviction policy, meaning the least-accessed items are removed first when memory pressure rises.

terms.definition: The primary interface for the in-memory cache. Provides Get, Set, TryGetValue, and Remove methods.
Fluent options object that controls absolute or sliding expiration, eviction callbacks, and cache entry priority.
An entry expires only if it has not been accessed within a specified time window. Each access resets the timer.
An entry expires at a fixed point in time regardless of how often it is accessed.

data.text: Register the service in Program.cs, then inject IMemoryCache into any controller, minimal API endpoint, or service. The TryGetValue pattern avoids the double-lookup problem by checking and returning in a single operation.

data.title: Registering IMemoryCache
data.content: Add the memory cache service to the DI container in Program.cs. This makes IMemoryCache available everywhere.

data.title: Caching with TryGetValue
data.content: The canonical caching pattern: try to get the cached value first, and only compute it if the cache miss occurs.

data.title: IMemoryCache is per-instance
data.text: IMemoryCache stores data in the local process. If your app runs on multiple servers or you scale out with Kubernetes, each instance maintains its own separate cache. Use IDistributedCache with Redis when you need a shared cache across instances.

Cache entries leave memory in three ways: they expire, they are evicted under memory pressure, or the code explicitly removes them. RegisterPostEvictionCallback lets you react to every eviction event — useful for logging, metrics, or refreshing data asynchronously.

data.caption: How a request flows through IMemoryCache
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Client Request] --> B{TryGetValue}
    B -->|Hit| C[Return Cached Data]
    B -->|Miss| D[Fetch from Database]
    D --> E[Set Cache Entry]
    E --> F[Return Data to Client]
    C --> F
    G[Expiration Timer] --> H[Remove Entry]
    H --> I[Post-Eviction Callback Fires]

data.title: Good Use Cases
items: Caching reference data that rarely changes (lookup tables, country codes)
Caching the result of expensive computations within a single server deployment
Reducing database round-trips for read-heavy endpoints
Storing per-request state without using HttpContext.Items

data.title: Avoid When
items: Your app runs on multiple servers and needs consistent cache state
You need cache persistence across application restarts
Cache size exceeds the memory budget of a single process

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: IMemoryCache lives in the local process — fast but not shared
Use TryGetValue + Set as the canonical caching pattern
Configure absolute and sliding expiration on each entry
Post-eviction callbacks let you react when entries leave memory
Switch to IDistributedCache when scaling beyond a single instance
data.takeaway: IMemoryCache is the simplest performant option for single-instance ASP.NET Core apps.

items.question: What is the default size limit for IMemoryCache?
items.answer: There is no default size limit unless you set one via options.SizeLimit. Without a limit, the cache can grow unbounded until the runtime evicts entries under memory pressure.

items.question: Is IMemoryCache thread-safe?
items.answer: Yes. The MemoryCache implementation is fully thread-safe. You can call Get and Set from concurrent requests without additional locking.
